content: The Integrated Management of Childhood Illness (IMCI) chart booklet allows for the classification of a child into one or more categories based on their health status. For each child, it is important to determine whether the findings recorded by the health worker (HW) and the reference evaluator (RE) are consistent. If all classifications agree, the answer is Yes. The overall agreement score is calculated as a percentage of the total possible score (45). Key definitions include: Missed responses: Cases where the RE records Yes, but the HW records No or Not Recorded (NR). Agreement: Cases where HW findings match those of the RE. If no data is recorded (NR), agreement is considered No. Clinical Observations and Classifications: 1. Severe Dehydration: A child may exhibit lethargy or irritability, sunken eyes, and slow skin pinch response. 2. Signs of Maltreatment: Physical Abuse: Includes bruises, lacerations, abrasions, scars, bite marks, fractures, burns, or head/spinal injuries. Injuries or Harm: Includes poisoning, non-fatal drowning, unusual medical service attendance, or fabricated/induced illness. Sexual Abuse: Includes anogenital symptoms or sexually transmitted infections. Neglect: Includes failure to provide basic needs, malnutrition, delayed treatment, or lack of care. Emotional Changes: Parents may report significant behavioral or emotional changes, recurrent nightmares, extreme distress, or oppositional behavior. Environmental Hygiene in Outpatient Clinics: 1. Observe handwashing facilities, toilets, and equipment in outpatient rooms, vaccination rooms, and treatment areas. 2. Record the availability and cleanliness of sinks, soap, and hand-drying materials. 3. 4. Evaluate the functionality and cleanliness of toilets for clients and staff, including accessibility for individuals with reduced mobility. 5. Assess the availability and condition of sharps containers, medical waste containers, and general waste containers. Essential Medicines and Supplies: 1. Review the availability and storage of essential medicines and supplies for child health services. 2. Verify that medicines are stored under appropriate conditions (15–25°C or up to 30°C depending on climate) and are functional on the day of review. 3. Assess stock records to monitor availability and identify stock-outs or reduced availability over the past 12 months. Policies, Guidelines, and Standards: 1. 2. Verify that staff have been oriented on these policies and use them routinely. 3. Confirm that protocols for managing sick children align with international or WHO standards, including danger signs, dehydration assessment, diarrhea management, respiratory assessment, fever evaluation, and referral protocols. Staff Training: 1. Identify all staff working in outpatient child health clinics and document their training history over the past five years. 2. Record the proportion of staff trained in key areas such as IMCI, nutrition, HIV/TB, childhood disabilities, and maltreatment. 3. Summarize findings and calculate the percentage of trained staff by category (e.g., doctors, nurses). Facility Action Plan: 1. Consolidate findings from checklists and identify strengths and areas for improvement. 2. Prioritize two or three key areas for improvement over the next three months. 3. Develop an action plan addressing underlying reasons for gaps, assign responsibilities, and set timelines. 4. Debrief with the facility director and staff to agree on findings and the action plan. Monitoring and Evaluation: 1. Review data from facility registers and health management information systems (HMIS) to validate reported data. 2. Identify discrepancies and discuss potential reasons with staff. 3. Use findings to develop an annual implementation plan for improving child health services, focusing on clinical practice, environmental hygiene, essential supplies, and staff training. Summary: The IMCI framework emphasizes accurate classification, consistent documentation, and adherence to clinical and operational standards. Regular monitoring, staff training, and action planning are critical to improving the quality of care for infants and young children in outpatient settings.
